statement: Shortest paths in a graph with negative edge weights can be computed by adding a large enough constant c to every edge weight to make all weights nonnegative, running Dijkstra, and then subtracting c once per edge used along the returned path.
definitions: Directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle (so shortest paths are well defined); c is any constant with c >= -(minimum edge weight); the procedure's output is Dijkstra's path in the shifted graph together with its shifted cost minus c times its number of edges; the claim asserts this equals a true shortest path and its cost.
ground_truth_witness: Directed graph s,a,b,t with edges s->t weight 0, s->a weight -1, a->b weight -1, b->t weight 1 (a DAG, no negative cycle). True shortest s->t is s->a->b->t of cost -1. The minimum weight is -1, so c=1; shifted weights are s->t = 1, s->a = 0, a->b = 0, b->t = 2. In the shifted graph Dijkstra picks the direct edge s->t at cost 1 (the 3-hop path now costs 0+0+2 = 2). Un-shifting by its own hop count gives 1 - 1*1 = 0, not -1, and the wrong path. The shift penalises paths by c per edge, so it reorders paths of different hop counts.
reference_authority: online-cited counterexample (MO/MSE/CS.SE/Wikipedia) with verify script, verified per partB_feasibility records

skeptic.objection: Reference verified: s->t 0, s->a -1, a->b -1, b->t 1 (DAG, no negative cycle); with c=1 Dijkstra returns s->t at shifted cost 1, unshifted 0, while the true shortest s->a->b->t costs -1; the failure persists for every c>=1 (direct edge wins iff c>1/2). Claim is precise once one notes shortest paths must be well defined (no negative cycles). Standard CS.SE folklore; solver needs a small 2-path-vs-1-path construction. Nothing on shortest paths in roster.
